title: Greens senator Jordon Steele-John takes leave amid investigation into complaints
content_c:
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the party room after complaints were made, triggering an independent review.
The Nine newspapers reported on Thursday afternoon that seven party members demanded an investigation into allegations he made inappropriate comments to a number of women between 2017 and 2025.
Steele-John said he rejected the claims and had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.
“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” he said in a statement.
“These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly. If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it.”
New Greens leader David Shoebridge said Steele-John had requested leave from the party room “and I have accepted it”.
Shoebridge said the party took “concerns of this nature extremely seriously”.
“This matter needs to be resolved via a fair and independent review that ensures all parties are entitled to natural justice and procedural fairness,” he said.
“The Australian Greens take complaints seriously, and as leader I want to make it clear that the integrity of the complaints process is essential.”
Guardian Australia has approached the Greens for further comment.
In his statement, Steele-John also said: “The letter says that victims of sexual and family violence should be at the centre of any investigation. I agree. In the one complaint of which I have been made aware, I am the person who experienced family violence.”
Born in England, Steele-John joined the upper house as a senator for Western Australia at the age of 22 in 2017 after the former Greens senator Scott Ludlam resigned after finding out he was a dual citizen.
He has been the party’s disability spokesperson since 2019 and has previously been the spokesperson for defence and nuclear.
Shoebridge was a member of the NSW parliament’s upper house until 2022.
When asked whether he was “ever aware of allegations or rumours of allegations against” Steele-John, Shoebridge replied: “No, I received the correspondence in my capacity as leader of the Australian Greens, and I’ve dealt with it with the urgency.”

title: Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
content_c:
Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
October 14, 2026
Albania's Education Ministry caught fire on Wednesday in a second day of student protests over corruption and education.
The scenes were at least somewhat reminiscent of the protracted student demonstrations in France in recent weeks.
They are probably the most violent outburst of low-level anti-corruption protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and the main opposition led by Sali Barisha that started in May this year.
What happened in Tirana's student protests?
Police deployed riot police and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds in the capital Tirana.
Thousands of protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry on Wednesday, many obscuring their faces. Some threw bricks at the building, damaged barriers on the sidewalks and overturned trash cans.
A bank near the Education Ministry also caught fire, according to the Reuters news agency citing a witness.
The demonstration started on Tuesday with a peaceful gathering of several hundred people outside the Education Ministry but quickly escalated and turned violent in places.
Police early on Wednesday reported around 40 detentions and 13 people injured, including six police officers. Unrest continued long after these figures were issued.
Government says demonstrations degenerated into 'orchestrated violence'
Deputy Prime Minster Albana Kociu posted a video of demonstrations on Facebook saying it was "disheartening to see the culture of protest degenerate into orchestrated violence."
She said that the attacks on institutions and police and the "senseless destruction of public property" were "not the language through which the youth should express themselves." Instead, she said they were reminiscent of the "old habits of those who use young people to mask their own political incompetence."
In another post, Kociu called on students who believe in the right to protest to "distance" themselves from "violence and vandalism."
Student organizers say the protests revolve around conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
More generally, Albania has faced a series of demonstrations this year sometimes referred to as the "Flamingo Revolution." These were at least partly prompted by a controversial construction project on the Adriatic Coast in a protected area where flamingos live.
But these partly environmental protests have also had a more general theme of dissatisfaction with Albania's dominant political forces. PM Edi Rama's Socialists and Sali Barisha's right-wing Democrats have alternated in government for more than 30 years, ever since the post-Cold War democratic transition in the former communist country.
The timing is also conspicuous, with the demonstrations starting amid prominent international coverage of widespread school and student protests in France in recent weeks leading to similarly restless scenes.
Edited by: Wesley Dockery

title: Geheimdienst-Reform: Deutschlands riskante Spionage-Pläne - Podcast
content_c:
Nachrichtendienste Deutschlands riskante Spionagepläne
Die deutschen Geheimdienste galten lange als harmlos und verschlafen. Nun will die Bundesregierung BND und Verfassungsschutz deutlich schlagkräftiger machen. BND-Präsident Martin Jäger warnte Anfang Oktober, von keinem anderen Land gehe eine so direkte und umfassende Bedrohung für Deutschland aus wie von Russland.
Die geplante Reform soll den Diensten erlauben, selbst aktiv gegen Gefahren vorzugehen. Möglich würden dadurch etwa Sabotageaktionen im Ausland und sogenannte Hackbacks gegen Cyberangriffe. Geheimdienste könnten dann etwa gestohlene deutsche Daten auf ausländischen Servern löschen oder technische Systeme des Gegners manipulieren.
Auch im Inland sollen die Befugnisse der Dienste ausgeweitet werden. Der Verfassungsschutz könnte dann Wohnungen heimlich betreten, Computer online untersuchen und mögliche Anschläge selbst abwehren. Bislang lag diese Aufgabe bei der Polizei. Kritiker sehen deshalb das Trennungsgebot zwischen Polizei und Nachrichtendiensten in Gefahr.
Der Blick in die USA zeigt, wie lang solche Befugnisse bestehen bleiben können, wenn sie einmal zur Abwehr einer bestimmten Gefahr ausgeweitet worden sind. Nach den Anschlägen vom 11. September erweiterte und verschärfte die US-Regierung ihre Anti-Terror-Instrumente. Und heute, zweieinhalb Jahrzehnte später, nutzt Donald Trump sie auch gegen vermeintliche Bedrohungen im Innern. Im Juni verurteilte die US-Justiz acht Demonstranten zu insgesamt 450 Jahren Haft und stützte sich dabei auf ein Gesetz aus dem Jahr 2001.
Die deutsche Reform berührt damit eine zentrale Frage des Rechtsstaats: Wie weit darf der Staat in die Freiheit seiner Bürgerinnen und Bürger engreifen, um ihre Sicherheit zu garantieren? Und wie verhindert er, dass Geheimdienste ihre Möglichkeiten missbrauchen?

Über diesen Podcast
Welche Folgen hat die neue Weltordnung für Deutschland? Und wie können wir uns in einer Welt behaupten, in der Herrscher wie Trump, Putin und Xi nach ihren eigenen Regeln spielen?
Das entschlüsseln die Hosts Britta Sandberg, langjährige Auslandskorrespondentin, und Christoph Hickmann, Leiter des Politikressorts, jede Woche im neuen SPIEGEL-Politikpodcast »MAD KINGS: Machtprobe für Deutschland«.

title: Ukraine kritisiert fehlende US-Unterstützung - NATO und EU widersprechen
content_c:
Russische Angriffe auf Kraftwerke Ukraine ohne US-Unterstützung? NATO und EU widersprechen
Die Ukraine ist beim Abwehrkampf gegen Russland auf Geheimdienstinformationen der USA angewiesen - doch die sollen vor neuen russischen Angriffen ausgeblieben sein. Präsident Selenskyj übt Kritik. EU und NATO beschwichtigen.
Russland hat erneut die Energieinfrastruktur der Ukraine attackiert. Alle drei Heizkraftwerke der Hauptstadt Kiew seien angegriffen worden, schrieb Ministerpräsident Serhij Korezkyj bei Telegram. Fünf Menschen kamen nach Angaben der Polizei in Kiew ums Leben. Zwei weitere Menschen starben nach Behördenangaben bei Attacken am Abend und in der Nacht im Gebiet Dnipropetrowsk. Mindestens 600.000 Menschen sind ohne Strom.
Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj und ranghohe Regierungsvertreter warfen den westlichen Verbündeten vor, die Ukraine vor den Angriffen nicht gewarnt zu haben. "Wieder einmal keine Vorwarnung von unseren Partnern", schrieb Selenskyj auf Facebook. Am Abend zuvor hätten die ukrainischen Systeme die russischen Raketen erst erfasst, als diese sich bereits der Hauptstadt Kiew näherten. "Das ist absolut ungerecht: Während sie unsere Infrastruktur zerstören, erhält die Ukraine noch nicht einmal Frühwarnungen über Raketenstarts."
Ein weiterer Regierungsvertreter sagte der Nachrichtenagentur AFP: "Es war bereits zweimal so, dass uns die Amerikaner nicht über den Start russischer Raketen informiert haben, als unser Energiesektor attackiert wurde." Es sei offensichtlich, dass sie Russland aus irgendeinem Grund helfen würden.
Starlink soll stark eingeschränkt gewesen sein
Zuvor hatte bereits der Technologieberater des Verteidigungsministeriums, Serhij Beskrestnow, erklärt, dass der Betrieb des US-Satelliten-Kommunikationssystems Starlink in der Nacht stark eingeschränkt gewesen sei, was zum Scheitern ukrainischer Angriffe geführt habe. Das habe der Ukraine "eine der wenigen Chancen" genommen, sich gegen neuartige, mit einem Strahltriebwerk ausgestattete Drohnen vom Typ Schahed zu wehren.
Die Ukraine ist in ihrem Abwehrkampf gegen Russland in hohem Maße auf westliche Geheimdienstinformationen angewiesen, insbesondere aus den USA. Ein US-Regierungsvertreter bestritt, dass sich die Position Washingtons gegenüber Kiew in Bezug auf den Austausch von Geheimdienstinformationen verändert habe.
Rutte ruft zu mehr Hilfe bei Flugabwehr auf
NATO-Generalsekretär Mark Rutte bestätigte zudem bei einem Besuch in Estland, dass US-Präsident Trump versichert habe, der Austausch der Informationen sei nicht gestoppt worden. Trump habe sich "sehr deutlich geäußert", sagte Rutte. Er rief die Verbündeten dazu auf, die Ukraine bei der Luftverteidigung stärker zu unterstützen.
Auch die EU erklärte, dass ihr "keine Anzeichen" dafür vorlägen, dass Washington die Weitergabe von Informationen eingestellt habe. Bundesaußenminister Johann Wadephul teilte ebenfalls mit, er erkenne nicht, dass es "eine substanzielle Verringerung" der US-Unterstützung gebe.
Verhältnis zwischen USA und Ukraine angespannt
Das russische Verteidigungsministerium bestätigte am Morgen Angriffe auf Kommunikations- und Energieinfrastruktur in der Hauptstadt Kiew und ihrem Umland sowie in der Region Charkiw. Alle Entwicklungen, die auf eine mögliche Änderung der US-Politik gegenüber der Ukraine hindeuteten, würden aufmerksam verfolgt. Es sei aber noch zu früh, Schlüsse zu ziehen, sagte Kreml-Sprecher Dmitri Peskow.
Das Verhältnis zwischen den USA und der Ukraine ist derzeit angespannt. Medienberichten zufolge hatte Washington zuletzt angedroht, die Weitergabe von militärischen Aufklärungsdaten zu stoppen, falls Kiew nicht kompromissbereiter werde.
Zudem hatte sich Starlink-Betreiber Elon Musk am Samstag hinter den US-Präsidenten gestellt. Er schrieb auf der Plattform X, Selenskyj sei mit seiner Reaktion auf eine Äußerung Trumps zu ukrainischen Gegenangriffen auf russische Raffinerien zu weit gegangen. Zuvor hatte Kiew ein Dieselabkommen zwischen den USA und Russland kritisiert.

title: Emotionen, Tempo, Härte: Der Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas
content_c:
Emotionen, Tempo, Härte: Der Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas
14. Oktober 2026
Für einen kurzen Moment war stille Betroffenheit zu spüren im sonst oft gnadenlosen politischen Berlin: Am Montag früh erklärte die Bundesarbeitsministerin und SPD-Vorsitzende Bärbel Bas ihren Rücktritt von allen Ämtern, auch den SPD-Vorsitz gibt sie auf. Die 58 Jahre alte Politikerin begründete ihren Schritt mit einem privaten Schicksalsschlag: "Nach dem Tod meiner Stieftochter habe ich festgestellt, dass ich Zeit brauche, um die Trauer zu verarbeiten", schrieb Bas in einer Erklärung.
Die Sozialdemokratin erklärte aber auch, die anhaltende Kritik an ihr von Seiten der Konservativen von CDU und CSU hätten zu ihrem Rückzug beigetragen. Wörtlich schrieb Bas, sie müsse "feststellen, dass die öffentlichen Angriffe auf mich, leider auch aus den Reihen des Koalitionspartners, in dieser für mich persönlich schwierigen Zeit weiter forciert wurden".
Merz sprach wohl in einem Hintergrund-Gespräch über Bas
Bas war zuletzt für die Umsetzung der komplizierten Reformen bei der staatlichen Rente zuständig - und wurde von einigen konservativen Politikern recht harsch aufgefordert, das Vorhaben nicht weiter zu verzögern. Glaubt man einem Bericht der "Süddeutschen Zeitung", dann soll vor allem ein Satz - ausgerechnet von Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU), gefallen in einem Hintergrund-Gespräch mit Journalisten - Bas sehr beschäftigt haben.
Eine Politikerin also, die sich privat und politisch so unter Druck gesetzt fühlt, dass sie lieber ihre Ämter aufgibt, als sich dem weiter auszusetzen? Der Berliner Politik- und Medienwissenschaftler Mirco Liefke beschäftigt sich schon lange mit Formen der öffentlichen Kommunikation.
Er sagt der DW, Unfairness und Härte habe es in der Politik schon immer gegeben, aber: "Was neu hinkommt, glaube ich schon, ist dieses Eskalations-Potenzial, die Geschwindigkeit, die durch die sozialen Medien in die Debatten gekommen ist. Und der Anreiz für einzelne Akteure, sich auch immer radikaler zu äußern."
Politik und Medien: Was ist öffentlich, was bleibt verborgen?
Emotionalität und Tempo sind also die treibenden Kräfte und die sozialen Medien eskalieren das mit ihren Algorithmen. Dazu gehört auch, dass es kaum noch Räume gibt, in denen Politiker Vertraulichkeit herstellen können. Merz soll sich in einem Hintergrundgespräch, aus dem eigentlich nicht berichtet werden darf, negativ über Bas geäußert haben.
Er erwähnte offenbar, Bas sei kaum noch präsent und lege keine eigenen Vorschläge vor. Obwohl ihm die private Situation der SPD-Chefin bekannt war. Ein Sprecher des Kanzlers wollte das weder bestätigen noch dementieren. Die Sätze waren da aber schon lange in der Welt. Liefke: "Es ist ein regelrechtes Geschäftsmodell geworden, eigentlich vertrauliche Inhalte durchzustechen und damit Aufmerksamkeit zu erzeugen."
Grünen-Chef Banaszak: "Keine Rückendeckung durch die SPD"
Der Grünen-Vorsitzende Felix Banaszak stammt wie Bas aus Duisburg in Nordrhein-Westfalen und kennt die bisherige SPD-Chefin seit vielen Jahren. Er sagt der DW: "Härte und Unerbittlichkeit sind nicht neu in der Politik. Aber es bleibt dabei, dass wir einen anderen Modus finden müssen, wenn wir die Menschen nicht immer weiter verschleißen wollen."
Banaszak nimmt auch die Kolleginnen und Kollegen der SPD in die Pflicht: "Dass Bärbel Bas aus den Reihen des Koalitionspartners so wenig Verständnis für ihre persönliche Situation erlebt hat, dass aber auch offenbar niemand in der SPD bereit war, sich in der Situation vor sie zu stellen und sie aus der Schusslinie zu nehmen, ist einfach kein gutes Zeichen."
Er sagt: "Es wäre naiv so zu tun, als wären die Angriffe auf einen Mann ähnlich gelaufen." Das sieht Wissenschaftler Liefke genauso: "Politikerinnen sind in einem wahnsinnigen Maße misogynen und sexualisierten Anfeindungen ausgesetzt, die in einer öffentlichen Sichtbarkeit ausgetragen werden, die neu ist."
CDU will Vorwürfe nicht auf sich sitzen lassen
Die Debatte um den richtigen Umgang mit Bärbel Bas und ihrer Trauer nahm nach ihrem Rückzug ähnliche Züge an wie vorher die Angriffe auf sie. Mecklenburg-Vorpommerns Ministerpräsidentin Manuela Schwesig (SPD) sprach von "unmenschlichen" Attacken aus der Union und erregte damit viele konservative Politiker. Kanzler Merz selbst zeigte sich öffentlich vom Rücktritt seiner Arbeitsministerin betroffen und wünschte ihr alles Gute.
Für Politikwissenschaftler Liefke ist das nur eine weitere Seite der Emotionalisierung. Zieht eine Politikerin die Konsequenzen, sei auch die Betroffenheit darüber höher als früher, auf allen Seiten: "Das ist ja im Grunde eine Fassade der Betroffenheit. Es hat etwas Rituelles, Reflexhaftes. Dass man dann so reagiert, weil man einem anderen Mega-Trend folgt: der Emotionalisierung."
Bas ist kein Einzelfall: Kevin Kühnert ist ein anderes Beispiel
Die Angriffe auf Bas sind nur ein Beispiel für den härter werden Ton in der politischen Debatte. Ordnungsrufe im Bundestag haben sprunghaft zugenommen, vor allem seit die in Teilen rechtsextreme "Alternative für Deutschland" (AfD) 2017 in das deutsche Parlament einzog. Schlagzeilen produzierten auch Rückzüge wie der von Kevin Kühnert (SPD).
Kühnert, früherer SPD-Generalsekretär, trat im Oktober 2024 zurück und gab dafür gesundheitliche Gründe an. Im April 2025 sagte er dann der Wochenzeitung "Die Zeit", er habe sich ständig aus dem rechtsextremistischen Spektrum bedroht gefühlt. Den politischen Debatten fehle es "zunehmend an Respekt für die Meinungen Andersdenkender".
Früherer Bundeskanzler Helmut Schmidt: öffentlich präsent - und doch privat
Mirco Liefke erinnert daran, wie es Politiker früher schafften, zwei getrennte Arten von Kommunikation auszuüben: eine öffentliche und eine private. "Wenn man an frühere Politiker-Generationen denkt, dann war es ja die Distanziertheit, das wenig emotional Aufgeladene eines Helmut Schmidt etwa, der nicht in Trauer verfallen ist angesichts der Dinge, die auf ihn eingeprasselt sind. Zumindest hat er das nicht nach außen gezeigt."
Schmidt (SPD) war von 1974 bis 1982 Bundeskanzler. Liefke analysiert: "Heute profitieren Politikerinnen wie Bärbel Bas von ihrer eigenen Biografie, wenn sie erzählen: 'Ich bin aus dem Arbeitermilieu und habe mich hochgearbeitet'. Davon profitieren sie, werden aber als Menschen viel sichtbarer und angreifbarer."
Ihr Bundestagsmandat will Bas, die von 2021 bis 2025 Bundestagspräsidentin war, behalten. Es dürfte ruhiger um sie werden - andere Personen werden im Mittelpunkt stehen, öffentlich und wohl auch privat.
description: Bundesarbeitsministern Bas hat ihr Amt niedergelegt. Sie begründet das mit einem Trauerfall in der Familie und der Härte innerhalb der Regierung. Warum sind öffentliche Debatten heute oft gnadenlos?

title: Графіки відключень світла 15 жовтня: до чого готуватися українцям
content_c:
Графіки відключень світла 15 жовтня: до чого готуватися українцям
«Укренерго» оголосило графіки відключень світла на 15 жовтня.
У четвер, 15 жовтня, у частині регіонів України запровадять відключення світла. Вони торкнуться як населення, так і підприємств.
Про це повідомила НЕК «Укренерго».
Графіки запроваджують через наслідки російських атак ракетами та дронами на енергооб’єкти. Обмеження діятимуть майже всю добу — від 06:00 до 23:59:
- Для промисловості та бізнесу запровадять графіки обмеження потужності.
- Для всіх категорій споживачів застосовуватимуть графіки погодинних відключень обсягом від 0,5 до 1,5 черги.
В «Укренерго» попередили, що через ризик нових обстрілів ситуація в енергосистемі може змінюватися. Споживачів просять стежити за оновленими графіками на сторінках своїх обленерго та ощадливо використовувати світло, коли воно є.
Відключення світла в Україні — останні новини
Нагадаємо, в Україні 14 жовтня діятимуть графіки відключення світла через наслідки російських атак на енергетичну інфраструктуру.
Також через нічну атаку росіян у п’яти районах Києва вранці відключили світло, а частина правого берега залишилася без електроенергії через аварію. Також у місті частково зупинявся громадський транспорт, а його маршрути довелося терміново змінювати.

У четвер, 15 жовтня, у частині регіонів України запровадять відключення світла. Вони торкнуться як населення, так і підприємств.
Про це повідомила НЕК «Укренерго».
Графіки запроваджують через наслідки російських атак ракетами та дронами на енергооб’єкти. Обмеження діятимуть майже всю добу — від 06:00 до 23:59:
- Для промисловості та бізнесу запровадять графіки обмеження потужності.
- Для всіх категорій споживачів застосовуватимуть графіки погодинних відключень обсягом від 0,5 до 1,5 черги.
В «Укренерго» попередили, що через ризик нових обстрілів ситуація в енергосистемі може змінюватися. Споживачів просять стежити за оновленими графіками на сторінках своїх обленерго та ощадливо використовувати світло, коли воно є.
Відключення світла в Україні — останні новини
Нагадаємо, в Україні 14 жовтня діятимуть графіки відключення світла через наслідки російських атак на енергетичну інфраструктуру.
Також через нічну атаку росіян у п’яти районах Києва вранці відключили світло, а частина правого берега залишилася без електроенергії через аварію. Також у місті частково зупинявся громадський транспорт, а його маршрути довелося терміново змінювати.

title: Эксперты назвали самые серьезные угрозы для здоровья человечества: две чреваты вымиранием
content_c:
Группа из десятков экспертов систематизировала данные о 17 серьезных угрозах здоровью населения планеты, с которыми человечество столкнулось в этом столетии. И главной темой их выводов стала готовность к подобным вызовам, сообщает Science Alert.
Несмотря на то что представленный обзор рисует тревожную картину, его главный посыл заключается в том, что риски глобальных катастроф можно снизить и взять под контроль — но лишь при условии, что общество начнет действовать уже сейчас.
«Поразительный вывод состоит не только в масштабах этих угроз, но и в том, что человечество по-прежнему способно действовать. Решения, принимаемые лидерами сегодня в отношении всех 17 катастрофических угроз, определят здоровье и благополучие следующего поколения», — заявил врач и специалист в области экономики здравоохранения Кристофер Дж. Л. Мюррей из Вашингтонского университета, сопредседатель Комиссии The Lancet по глобальным угрозам здоровью в XXI веке.
В ходе исследования ученые использовали моделирование, чтобы оценить, какого объема смертности и инвалидности можно было бы избежать в связи с каждой из этих угроз в период с 2025 по 2100 год. Результаты оценивали по шкале DALY (годы жизни, скорректированные с учетом нетрудоспособности). Этот показатель используется для оценки общего времени, которое население теряет из-за преждевременной смерти или жизни с болезнью, травмой либо инвалидностью. Иными словами, один DALY равен одному потерянному году «здоровой жизни».
Из 12 угроз ученые особенно выделили две, отметив, что они несут «риски вымирания» человечества до 2100 года.
«К числу таких угроз относятся злонамеренное использование искусственного интеллекта (в том числе для создания новых видов биологического оружия) и ядерный конфликт, способный привести к ядерному голоду», — заявили ученые. Они отметили, что другие угрозы, способные погубить человечество, например падение астероида или извержение супервулкана, не включили в список из-за крайне низкой вероятности их наступления в этом столетии.
Еще один гипотетический сценарий, способный привести к исчезновению человечества — создание «зеркальной формы жизни», — также был исключен из рассмотрения: эта технология пока не разработана, и, несмотря на теоретические риски для здоровья людей, оценивать их количественно пока преждевременно.
Еще 15 угроз оценили как такие, которые могут унести более миллиарда жизней. В этой категории исследователи выделили: загрязнение воздуха, устойчивость к противомикробным препаратам, недостаточное питание у детей, изменение климата, резкое сокращение международного финансирования здравоохранения, традиционные вооруженные конфликты, чрезмерное потребление алкоголя, высокое артериальное давление, неравенство доходов, низкий уровень образования, пандемии природного происхождения, ожирение, проблемы с психическим здоровьем, курение и нездоровое старение.
Ученые считают, что наибольшую угрозу, которую можно было бы предотвратить, несет ожирение. Разница между наилучшим и наихудшим сценариями к 2100 году оценивается в 23,1 миллиарда DALY, что сопоставимо примерно с 46 пандемиями COVID-19.
Согласно базовому прогнозу исследователей, совокупное глобальное бремя болезней и травм в период с 2025 по 2100 год оценивается в 246 миллиардов DALY, что эквивалентно примерно 500 пандемиям COVID-19.
Напомним, недавно ученые провели первое в своем роде исследование, в ходе которого назвали место на Земле, которое будет достаточно безопасным для того, чтобы переждать глобальный катаклизм любого рода.

title: На фронті відбулось 222 боїв за добу, найбільше на покровському напрямку – Генштаб
content_c:
Російські війська від початку доби 222 разів атакували позиції Сил оборони України, найактивнішим ворог був на покровському напрямку, повідомляє генеральний штаб Збройних сил України.
"Загалом від початку цієї доби відбулося 222 бойові зіткнення. Противник завдав одного ракетного удару та 58 авіаційних ударів, скинув 190 керованих авіабомб. Крім того, залучив для ураження 5221 дрон-камікадзе та здійснив 1736 обстрілів населених пунктів і позицій наших військ", – йдеться в повідомленні.
На північно-слобожанському та курському напрямках від початку доби окупанти провели дві штурмові дії, завдали одного авіаудару, застосувавши один КАБ, здійснили 44 обстріли позицій українських військ і населених пунктів, два з яких – із застосуванням РСЗВ.
На південно-слобожанському напрямку противник десять разів атакував позиції українських підрозділів у районах населених пунктів Ізбицьке, Тернова, Охрімівка, Чугунівка та в бік Захарівки, Чорного, Малої Вовчої. П'ять із цих штурмів ще тривають.
На куп'янському напрямку ворог 15 разів намагався покращити свої позиції, проводячи штурмові дії в бік Радьківки.
П'ять спроб загарбників просунутися відбивали на лиманському напрямку в бік населеного пункту Лиман та неподалік Масляківки.
На слов'янському напрямку Сили оборони зупинили дві спроби загарбників йти вперед у районі населеного пункту Крива Лука.
На костянтинівському напрямку Сили оборони відбивали 19 ворожих штурмів: у районі населеного пункту Костянтинівка та в бік Новоселівки, Миколайпілля, Новопавлівки, Торецького, Грузького, Вільного та Молодецького. Триває бій.
29 атак здійснив ворог на покровському напрямку. Окупанти намагалися просунутися неподалік населених пунктів Білицьке, Новий Донбас, Чернігівка, Світле, Добропілля, Новогришине, Гуліве, Сергіївка, Мирне, Молодецьке, Муравка та Новопавлівка.
"За попередніми підрахунками, сьогодні тут ліквідовано 68 окупантів, 14 – поранено; знищено 11 одиниць автомобільної техніки, чотири спеціальні засоби та три укриття. Пошкоджено дві одиниці автомобільної техніки, гармату, пункт управління БпЛА та 37 укриттів особового складу противника. Знищено або подавлено 164 безпілотні літальні апарати різних типів", – сказано в повідомленні.
На олександрівському напрямку ворог один раз штурмував у бік Березового.
На гуляйпільському напрямку Сили оборони відбили 13 ворожих атак у районах населених пунктів Рибне, Тернувате, Рівне, Воздвижівка, Гірке, Верхня Терса, Новоселівка та Омельник.
На оріхівському напрямку окупанти намагалися покращити своє становище, чотири рази атакуючи в бік Павлівки та Степногірська.

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
content_c:
US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
- Published
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.
The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.
Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher petrol prices, which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The elections are being fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
What causes inflation?
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
What is the current rate of inflation?
Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.
Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.
In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.
Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.
At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.
Will the inflation hike change Social Security payments?
Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.
The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.
The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.
How have tariffs affected inflation?
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
Has inflation been worse lately?
While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
Can inflation ever go down?
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

What is inflation?
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
What causes inflation?
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

title: 'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
content_c:
'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
- Published
Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years.
The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything".
She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise.
Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers for September that were released on Wednesday. The price rise was more than economists and Wall Street analysts had forecast.
High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans.
Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family.
"I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark."
Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money.
And it is still not enough to support her family.
Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home.
"I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said.
The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult.
And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline.
"I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (£4.5)," he said.
Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control."
He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up.
The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, the index was -40. In May, it reached -45, the lowest since 2022.
A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis.
This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that.
When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef."
As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said.
Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken.
"[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said.
Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month.
"I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically."
For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming.
She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies.
Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice.
The family has even decided to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much.
"It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot."

title: Thursday briefing: Thanks to an erratic Trump, peace in Ukraine is still far away
content_c:
Good morning. In his usual asinine unconventional approach to international relations, Donald Trump announced on Sunday (via Truth Social, how else) an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”, apparently without checking with either side. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said any such deal was “news to me,” nonetheless declared he was “ready and we will accept it”. Vladimir Putin responded by blowing up some Ukrainian power plants.
This has been the tenor of much diplomacy during Trump’s tenure: false starts, U-turns, incoherent positions (and some playful flirting with Vlad). Meanwhile fighting continues, and America’s allies attempt to manage the fallout. Andy Burnham hosted Zelenskyy at Downing Street yesterday, stating the UK is doubling down on its support for Ukraine, and pointedly calling on others to “follow suit”.
It’s a negotiators nightmare. So how are ambassadors, spooks and diplomats handling the chaos? Is an actual ceasefire or peace deal within their grasp? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to career diplomat and former ambassador Nigel Gould-Davies to find out. Before that, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK | Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
- 
  Gaza | Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.
- 
  EU | Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
- 
  Ukraine | Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to immediately halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry.
- 
  Vaccine | Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said.
In depth: ‘A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests’
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, efforts to secure either a temporary ceasefire or a permanent peace deal have resolutely failed. Endless rounds of talks in Belarus, Turkey, Abu Dhabi and Geneva have all proved futile. To Nigel Gould-Davies, it’s obvious why. A former British diplomat, he was head of economics at the Foreign Office in Moscow before his stint as the UK’s ambassador to Belarus. Today, he is senior fellow for Russia and Eurasia at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
Gould-Davies tells me that there are established norms for negotiating during military conflicts. Diplomats look for the interests, needs and red lines that each side articulates, in pursuit of the elusive “win set”.
“A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests to end the fighting than to continue,” he says. “You have to find that overlap in the Venn diagram that leads to a defined set of conditions which, despite involving painful compromises, is ultimately judged to better serve each side than continuing to fight.
“The problem with this situation is that Russia has no interest in ending the war,” he says. Tricky to find common ground, then.
It is through this lens that we should view all Russia-Ukraine talks since Trump’s return to the presidency, Gould-Davies suggests. “They have not really been negotiations,” but “parallel efforts by Russia and Ukraine to persuade the White House it’s the other side’s fault” that a peace agreement (and, perhaps more importantly to Trump, that elusive Nobel peace prize) had failed to materialise. 
  That said, the respective red lines aren’t difficult to identify. Ukraine has time and again said it is willing to accept an unconditional ceasefire. “Russia, by contrast, has repeatedly said publicly that it is not interested in a ceasefire,” says Gould-Davies, only in a full and final end to the war that, in Russian terms, means “decisive superiority and dominance over a severely weakened Ukraine”.
That’s an outcome Ukraine can’t, and won’t, sign up for.
The ‘non-standard president’
This is already a headache for UK, European and American diplomats, who most recently met in Miami at the end of last week. But there’s also the added Trump-shaped impediment to grapple with; what Gould-Davies diplomatically describes as the challenge of having “a non-standard president” in the White House. When Trump unilaterally declared an energy ceasefire, Gould-Davies says, it had “no basis whatsoever in reality”. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv was aware. “He simply made it up … a product of a fantasy.”
The botched digital diplomacy aside, Trump’s interests also don’t appear aligned with Ukraine or traditional US allies. “[Trump’s] natural centre of gravity is to favour Russia,” says Gould-Davies, citing restrictions on US weapons supplies and past pauses in intelligence sharing. Yesterday, Zelenskyy accused Trump of restricting Ukrainian access to “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences.
Granted, Trump has at times sided with the Ukrainian president: sanctioning Russian oil companies and helping Ukraine target Russian energy infrastructure. But for all Trump’s “lurching”, says Gould-Davies, his theory of ending the war involves concessions to Russia and coercion of Ukraine.
The price of a deal
After a period of relative quiet from Trump on the Russia-Ukraine front, this week Trump’s attention returned. With Americans facing soaring energy costs, he announced a plan to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down pump prices, much to the dismay not just of European leaders but a bipartisan group of US senators, too.
Leave aside, for a second, suggestions that these imports could be illegal under American law and that quantities being discussed are seemingly too small to actually affect prices, even if the fuel could reach the US ahead of next month’s midterms, as Trump hopes.
In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal “is only the visible tip of the iceberg”, says Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a “much more substantial” pro-Russia tilt.
Gould-Davies suspects that Trump could be, via Russia, seeking to get Iran to ease the blockade on the strait of Hormuz, in the hope of actually bringing down fuel prices before American voters head to the polls. Putin’s quid pro quo for brokering these efforts, Gould-Davies says, “could be an easing of America’s sanctions on Russia and an ending to America’s support for Ukraine”.
It’s just a theory, he caveats, “but join the dots and it logically makes sense”.
Either way, for diplomats it’s just further proof that Trump’s mercurial methods are more a hindrance than help.
The quiet work behind the scenes
Nonetheless, diplomatic back channels remain operational: secret, closed-door meetings and off-the-record communications between all sides. Not that Gould-Davies thinks they’re worth the effort. “There is a degree of collective delusion here,” he says: “A hope that Russia can somehow be persuaded” to change course, for which “there is literally no evidence for that whatsoever”. He worries that these informal discussions could even be “actively unhelpful, because they perpetuate the illusion that peace may be around the corner”.
And, while Europe might traditionally have focused its diplomatic efforts in hostile territory, attention has now turned towards the US itself. There’s still hope that Trump’s whispers might pay further dividends. As Gould-Davies puts it, this “Avengers assemble” approach has seen European leaders and diplomats descend on Washington when Trump’s veered too far off course. For all the tumult, he says, this has proved effective in averting “the nightmare scenario” of Trump binning off America’s old transatlantic partners for good.
But as fans of Netflix’s The Diplomat will know, even diplomacy between allies isn’t plain sailing. “Right now even ‘the White House’ is an abstraction,” says Gould-Davies. “It consists of many different players, plenty of whom have different views privately from President Trump.” Take John Ratcliffe, director of the CIA, who visited Moscow this summer. There is “reliable speculation”, says Gould-Davies, that he hoped to “warn Russia against escalation into Europe”. It’s a totally different note to those currently being struck by Trump.
“There are people in positions of power and influence still in this administration who understand the problem of Russia in the right way,” says Gould-Davies. With that in mind, western diplomats will continue to try to shift the balance of influences within the White House, but they’re reliant on what he labels a White House Kremlinology – “trying to understand the different views and moods of those around Trump and who will be the last person to whisper in his ear.”
What else we’ve been enjoying
- 
  How We Win is a new Guardian newsletter series featuring writers like Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan and Bernie Sanders on defeating Trumpism. Read Robert Reich’s introduction to the project here, and then sign up here to get each week’s piece directly to your inbox. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team
- 
  Are you a Hannah, a Marnie, a Jess or a Shoshanna? Or did Lena Dunham’s Girls pass you by the first time round? If it did, then this excellent piece by Louis Staples (a Marnie) may well convince you to binge the whole thing in time for the recently announced five-episode revival. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team
- 
  In another of our newsletters, The Long Wave, Micha Frazer-Carroll writes about taking up Jamaican Patois classes and what learning the language taught her about shame and her connection to her ancestry. Charlie
- 
  I look forward to the Wildlife photographer of the year exhibition every year, and this year’s winning images didn’t disappoint. You can see a selection of them here, including my favourite: James Lewin’s dream-like shot of a young bull elephant giving a zebra an impromptu shower. Lucinda
- 
  Rachel Dixon on our travel desk has pulled together this beautiful list of Britain’s best heated lidos to keep you swimming through winter. Move over WFH, and hello WFHL? Charlie
Sport
Champions League | Paris Saint-Germain romped to a 4-2 victory over Manchester City, while Bradley Barcola hit his first Liverpool goals with a hat-trick in a 6-3 win over Lask. Elsewhere, Aston Villa demolished Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park.
Fifa | Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and awarding Donald Trump the Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting on Thursday.
Formula One | Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join its calendar, having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s.
The front pages
The Guardian splashes on “Zelenskyy blames Trump for loss of protection from Russian raids”. The Times has “Zelensky: My people will die after Trump betrayal”, the Telegraph runs “More on benefits at age seven than age 50” and top story at the Financial Times is “Jump in US inflation deepens pain for voters ahead of key midterm elections”.
Elsewhere, focus is on the Russell Brand trial. Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Reporting the prosecution’s opening statement, the Sun headlines with the quote “‘Ruthless calculated sexual predator’”, The i Paper also headlines with “Brand a ‘ruthless and calculated sexual predator’”, the Mail has “The ‘predator’ in sunglasses” and The Mirror leads with the quote “‘Predator’”.
The Latest
India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown
A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims that it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters. But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that the country is sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to the south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen – watch on YouTube
Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
On Copenhagen’s rooftops live 80 to 100 colonies of honeybees, tended by a collective of beekeepers called Bybi.
Set up in 2010 with the aim of employing marginalised people, Bybi’s work has evolved into a response to the modern economic system.
With the help of volunteers, from refugees to people on incapacity benefits, they produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year, which they sell (often letting people pay what they like) or give away, asking that people share it with loved ones and plant a flower to help the bees. They also run schools programmes, supported by sponsorships from universities and corporations.
“Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection,” says founder Oliver Maxwell, “asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
Bored at work?
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

content:
Good morning. In his usual asinine unconventional approach to international relations, Donald Trump announced on Sunday (via Truth Social, how else) an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”, apparently without checking with either side. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said any such deal was “news to me,” nonetheless declared he was “ready and we will accept it”. Vladimir Putin responded by blowing up some Ukrainian power plants.
This has been the tenor of much diplomacy during Trump’s tenure: false starts, U-turns, incoherent positions (and some playful flirting with Vlad). Meanwhile fighting continues, and America’s allies attempt to manage the fallout. Andy Burnham hosted Zelenskyy at Downing Street yesterday, stating the UK is doubling down on its support for Ukraine, and pointedly calling on others to “follow suit”.
It’s a negotiators nightmare. So how are ambassadors, spooks and diplomats handling the chaos? Is an actual ceasefire or peace deal within their grasp? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to career diplomat and former ambassador Nigel Gould-Davies to find out. Before that, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  UK | Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
- 
  Gaza | Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.
- 
  EU | Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
- 
  Ukraine | Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to immediately halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry.
- 
  Vaccine | Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said.
In depth: ‘A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests’
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, efforts to secure either a temporary ceasefire or a permanent peace deal have resolutely failed. Endless rounds of talks in Belarus, Turkey, Abu Dhabi and Geneva have all proved futile. To Nigel Gould-Davies, it’s obvious why. A former British diplomat, he was head of economics at the Foreign Office in Moscow before his stint as the UK’s ambassador to Belarus. Today, he is senior fellow for Russia and Eurasia at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
Gould-Davies tells me that there are established norms for negotiating during military conflicts. Diplomats look for the interests, needs and red lines that each side articulates, in pursuit of the elusive “win set”.
“A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests to end the fighting than to continue,” he says. “You have to find that overlap in the Venn diagram that leads to a defined set of conditions which, despite involving painful compromises, is ultimately judged to better serve each side than continuing to fight.
“The problem with this situation is that Russia has no interest in ending the war,” he says. Tricky to find common ground, then.
It is through this lens that we should view all Russia-Ukraine talks since Trump’s return to the presidency, Gould-Davies suggests. “They have not really been negotiations,” but “parallel efforts by Russia and Ukraine to persuade the White House it’s the other side’s fault” that a peace agreement (and, perhaps more importantly to Trump, that elusive Nobel peace prize) had failed to materialise. 
  That said, the respective red lines aren’t difficult to identify. Ukraine has time and again said it is willing to accept an unconditional ceasefire. “Russia, by contrast, has repeatedly said publicly that it is not interested in a ceasefire,” says Gould-Davies, only in a full and final end to the war that, in Russian terms, means “decisive superiority and dominance over a severely weakened Ukraine”.
That’s an outcome Ukraine can’t, and won’t, sign up for.
The ‘non-standard president’
This is already a headache for UK, European and American diplomats, who most recently met in Miami at the end of last week. But there’s also the added Trump-shaped impediment to grapple with; what Gould-Davies diplomatically describes as the challenge of having “a non-standard president” in the White House. When Trump unilaterally declared an energy ceasefire, Gould-Davies says, it had “no basis whatsoever in reality”. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv was aware. “He simply made it up … a product of a fantasy.”
The botched digital diplomacy aside, Trump’s interests also don’t appear aligned with Ukraine or traditional US allies. “[Trump’s] natural centre of gravity is to favour Russia,” says Gould-Davies, citing restrictions on US weapons supplies and past pauses in intelligence sharing. Yesterday, Zelenskyy accused Trump of restricting Ukrainian access to “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences.
Granted, Trump has at times sided with the Ukrainian president: sanctioning Russian oil companies and helping Ukraine target Russian energy infrastructure. But for all Trump’s “lurching”, says Gould-Davies, his theory of ending the war involves concessions to Russia and coercion of Ukraine.
The price of a deal
After a period of relative quiet from Trump on the Russia-Ukraine front, this week Trump’s attention returned. With Americans facing soaring energy costs, he announced a plan to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down pump prices, much to the dismay not just of European leaders but a bipartisan group of US senators, too.
Leave aside, for a second, suggestions that these imports could be illegal under American law and that quantities being discussed are seemingly too small to actually affect prices, even if the fuel could reach the US ahead of next month’s midterms, as Trump hopes.
In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal “is only the visible tip of the iceberg”, says Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a “much more substantial” pro-Russia tilt.
Gould-Davies suspects that Trump could be, via Russia, seeking to get Iran to ease the blockade on the strait of Hormuz, in the hope of actually bringing down fuel prices before American voters head to the polls. Putin’s quid pro quo for brokering these efforts, Gould-Davies says, “could be an easing of America’s sanctions on Russia and an ending to America’s support for Ukraine”.
It’s just a theory, he caveats, “but join the dots and it logically makes sense”.
Either way, for diplomats it’s just further proof that Trump’s mercurial methods are more a hindrance than help.
The quiet work behind the scenes
Nonetheless, diplomatic back channels remain operational: secret, closed-door meetings and off-the-record communications between all sides. Not that Gould-Davies thinks they’re worth the effort. “There is a degree of collective delusion here,” he says: “A hope that Russia can somehow be persuaded” to change course, for which “there is literally no evidence for that whatsoever”. He worries that these informal discussions could even be “actively unhelpful, because they perpetuate the illusion that peace may be around the corner”.
And, while Europe might traditionally have focused its diplomatic efforts in hostile territory, attention has now turned towards the US itself. There’s still hope that Trump’s whispers might pay further dividends. As Gould-Davies puts it, this “Avengers assemble” approach has seen European leaders and diplomats descend on Washington when Trump’s veered too far off course. For all the tumult, he says, this has proved effective in averting “the nightmare scenario” of Trump binning off America’s old transatlantic partners for good.
But as fans of Netflix’s The Diplomat will know, even diplomacy between allies isn’t plain sailing. “Right now even ‘the White House’ is an abstraction,” says Gould-Davies. “It consists of many different players, plenty of whom have different views privately from President Trump.” Take John Ratcliffe, director of the CIA, who visited Moscow this summer. There is “reliable speculation”, says Gould-Davies, that he hoped to “warn Russia against escalation into Europe”. It’s a totally different note to those currently being struck by Trump.
“There are people in positions of power and influence still in this administration who understand the problem of Russia in the right way,” says Gould-Davies. With that in mind, western diplomats will continue to try to shift the balance of influences within the White House, but they’re reliant on what he labels a White House Kremlinology – “trying to understand the different views and moods of those around Trump and who will be the last person to whisper in his ear.”
What else we’ve been enjoying
- 
  How We Win is a new Guardian newsletter series featuring writers like Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan and Bernie Sanders on defeating Trumpism. Read Robert Reich’s introduction to the project here, and then sign up here to get each week’s piece directly to your inbox. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team
- 
  Are you a Hannah, a Marnie, a Jess or a Shoshanna? Or did Lena Dunham’s Girls pass you by the first time round? If it did, then this excellent piece by Louis Staples (a Marnie) may well convince you to binge the whole thing in time for the recently announced five-episode revival. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team
- 
  In another of our newsletters, The Long Wave, Micha Frazer-Carroll writes about taking up Jamaican Patois classes and what learning the language taught her about shame and her connection to her ancestry. Charlie
- 
  I look forward to the Wildlife photographer of the year exhibition every year, and this year’s winning images didn’t disappoint. You can see a selection of them here, including my favourite: James Lewin’s dream-like shot of a young bull elephant giving a zebra an impromptu shower. Lucinda
- 
  Rachel Dixon on our travel desk has pulled together this beautiful list of Britain’s best heated lidos to keep you swimming through winter. Move over WFH, and hello WFHL? Charlie
Sport
Champions League | Paris Saint-Germain romped to a 4-2 victory over Manchester City, while Bradley Barcola hit his first Liverpool goals with a hat-trick in a 6-3 win over Lask. Elsewhere, Aston Villa demolished Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park.
Fifa | Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and awarding Donald Trump the Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting on Thursday.
Formula One | Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join its calendar, having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s.
The front pages
The Guardian splashes on “Zelenskyy blames Trump for loss of protection from Russian raids”. The Times has “Zelensky: My people will die after Trump betrayal”, the Telegraph runs “More on benefits at age seven than age 50” and top story at the Financial Times is “Jump in US inflation deepens pain for voters ahead of key midterm elections”.
Elsewhere, focus is on the Russell Brand trial. Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Reporting the prosecution’s opening statement, the Sun headlines with the quote “‘Ruthless calculated sexual predator’”, The i Paper also headlines with “Brand a ‘ruthless and calculated sexual predator’”, the Mail has “The ‘predator’ in sunglasses” and The Mirror leads with the quote “‘Predator’”.
The Latest
India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown
A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims that it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters. But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that the country is sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to the south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen – watch on YouTube
Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
On Copenhagen’s rooftops live 80 to 100 colonies of honeybees, tended by a collective of beekeepers called Bybi.
Set up in 2010 with the aim of employing marginalised people, Bybi’s work has evolved into a response to the modern economic system.
With the help of volunteers, from refugees to people on incapacity benefits, they produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year, which they sell (often letting people pay what they like) or give away, asking that people share it with loved ones and plant a flower to help the bees. They also run schools programmes, supported by sponsorships from universities and corporations.
“Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection,” says founder Oliver Maxwell, “asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
Bored at work?
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

title: Climate change and drone attacks exacerbate the humanitarian crisis in war-torn Sudan
content_c:
Climate change, drone attacks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis
October 14, 2026
In Sudan, clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season.
Since war broke out between the two factions and their allied militias in April 2023, both sides have fought for power. However, neither has managed to establish control over the entire country.
The SAF, the nation's official army, is in control of Sudan's north and center, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF maintains its presence in the western Darfur region and parts of the south.
The brutal war has plunged Sudan into one of the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crises, according to the United Nations and international aid organizations. The estimated death toll ranges from 40,000 to 250,000 people as reliable figures remain difficult to obtain amid the ongoing fighting. More than 12.4 million Sudanese have also been displaced, both within Sudan and to neighboring countries.
This week, the aid organization Action Against Hunger sounded the alarm.
"24.6 million people are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity," Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, executive director of the German section of the NGO, told DW.
Friedrich-Rust added that an estimated 825,000 children younger than 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, while a total of 4.2 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women are thought to be acutely malnourished.
In October, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) — which monitors food insecurity and uses the internationally recognized Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system — also warned that several areas including camps for internally displaced people in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, are expected to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), the most severe classification of acute food insecurity.
"The situation in Sudan continues to deteriorate and humanitarian needs are growing, even as the resources to respond are shrinking," Fabrizia Falcione, the Sudan representative of the United Nations Population Fund, the UN agency for sexual and reproductive health, said.
"I recently visited the displacement camp Tawila and I am still struggling to find the words to describe what I witnessed," Falcione told DW. "Imagine a population larger than that of Frankfurt, Germany, forced to flee their homes and seek refuge in one place in less than three years."
She added that more than 700,000 people there rely on just one hospital capable of performing Caesarean sections.
Despite repeated warnings about the deteriorating humanitarian situation, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which calls for $2.9 billion (€2.59 bn), is just 41% funded, with $1.2 billion (€1.07 bn) received from international donors so far.
Climate shocks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recently warned that extreme heat and heavy flooding are worsening the crisis in Sudan.
"This year, a massive heatwave brought power cuts of up to 12 hours per day in some regions," Hager Ali, a Sudan researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), told DW. "Riverbeds and dried-out fields are barren, which comes on top of the damage from combat, the RSF's scorched-earth tactics and environmental destruction."
While the drought is affecting roughly half the country, heavy rains and localized flooding have worsened conditions in other areas of Sudan.
"As if that wasn't enough, there is also a massive shortage of fertilizer and diesel," Ali told DW.
Sudan relies on imported fertilizer and diesel shipped from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. However, amid the wider Iran war, Iran has been blocking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have threatened and at times disrupted shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
"Fertilizer supply collapsed from 450,000 metric tons to only about 50,000" in 2026, Ali said, adding that a similar diesel shortage and the soaring cost of diesel compound the situation in two ways.
"Agricultural equipment uses diesel and the transportation of humanitarian and agricultural goods within the country is getting a lot more expensive," Ali said.
In October, the International Food Policy Research Institute warned that staple food- and fuel prices in Sudan rose sharply in September 2026.
Limited arms embargo curbs hope for an end to the war
Observers have long pointed out that the war in Sudan will not end until foreign backers stop supplying arms. The SAF is officially supported by Egypt, Turkey, Russia and Iran while the United Arab Emirates is alleged to be the RSF's main backer, a claim Abu Dhabi denies.
However, in October, the UN Security Council extended the existing arms embargo only on Sudan's Darfur region until December 11, dropping calls for a nationwide embargo.
"To expand the UN embargo across Sudan would have included drones in particular," Hager Ali said, noting that Sudan is one of the biggest theaters for drone warfare: As of 2026, the leading cause of civilian casualties in Sudan are drone strikes.
She also told DW that Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed the extention of the embargo over concerns that it would disproportionately limit the Sudanese Armed Forces on the battlefield.
"An arms embargo would deter potential backers from cooperating with the Sudanese Armed Forces, whereas the Rapid Support Forces don't necessarily source their weapons through official ways," Hager Ali said.
"The RSF rely on trafficking with other militias, private military contractors and traders in the region," she said, adding that because the RSF obtains supplies from numerous sources and actors, it is difficult to target the group through a single embargo.
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

title: Kanzler setzt auf gute Regierungsarbeit gegen Extremismus
content_c:
Erklärung im Bundestag Merz setzt auf gute Regierungsarbeit gegen Extremismus
In seiner Regierungserklärung betont der Kanzler, dass Deutschland unter Druck stehe wie "vielleicht noch nie". Unzufriedenheit führe zu Extremismus. Dem müsse man "schöpferische Anstrengung" entgegensetzen.
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz will dem zunehmenden Extremismus in Deutschland gutes Regierungshandeln entgegensetzen. Die Gerechtigkeitslücke werde weiter wachsen, "wenn wir nicht handeln", sagte Merz in seiner Regierungserklärung im Bundestag.
Wo Extremismus "seine Wurzel in berechtigter Unzufriedenheit" und in "berechtigten Empfindungen von Ungerechtigkeit" habe, so Merz, da sei die einzige Antwort, "diese Zerstörungskraft zu etwas Gutem" umzuwandeln: Das Land brauche jetzt eine "schöpferische Anstrengung".
"Die haben wir aufzubringen und die werden wir aufbringen - auch und gerade gegen den Extremismus, (...) der gerade wieder in dieses Parlament eindringt und in die Landesparlamente eindringt und in die Alltagswelt unseres Landes", betonte der Kanzler. Deutschland stehe unter Druck "wie vielleicht noch nie seit seiner Gründung".
Chrupalla: Steuerzahler können sich Ukraine-Hilfen nicht mehr leisten
Damit spielte Merz auf die Erfolge der AfD bei den Landtagswahlen im September an, bei denen die AfD deutlich hinzugewonnen hatte und in Sachsen-Anhalt möglicherweise an die Regierung kommen wird. Er wandte sich in seiner Rede direkt an die AfD-Abgeordneten und kritisierte ihr "höhnisches Gelächter mit der Freude an der Zersetzung und an der Zerstörung".
Diese griffen Merz scharf an. AfD-Chef Tino Chrupalla warf dem Kanzler "politisches Versagen" vor. Nichts habe sich getan, sagte er mit Blick auf Bereiche wie Rente, Pflege oder Gesundheit. "Herr Bundeskanzler, Hand aufs Herz, das wird nichts mehr", sagte Chrupalla. Seine Co-Chefin Alice Weidel sagte: "Es ist vorbei, Herr Merz." Sie rief erneut dazu auf, Erdöl und Erdgas aus Russland zu beziehen.
Chrupalla forderte Merz auf, die "mittlerweile unendliche finanzielle und militärische Unterstützung" der Ukraine zu beenden. Die Steuerzahler könnten sich diese nicht mehr leisten.
Merz weist Behauptung der AfD entschieden zurück
Derartigen Forderungen hielt Merz entgegen: "Kein Euro, der in die Ukraine fließt, fehlt bei den Sozialausgaben und den Bildungsausgaben in unserem Land." Das sage er deutlich an die Adresse all derjenigen, die daraus "ein Gerechtigkeitsproblem konstruieren wollen".
Der Kanzler betonte, dass es für das Ziel eines friedlichen, freien, und sicheren Europa Investitionen in die Verteidigungsfähigkeit und den Abwehrkampf der Ukraine gegen die russischen Angriffe brauche. Nur so schaffe man die Voraussetzungen für Freiheit, die Rechtsstaat, Wirtschaft und Gemeinwesen bräuchten, damit sich Gerechtigkeit entfalten könne.
Merz warnte, dies alles sei sehr konkret in Gefahr und verwies auf eine steigende Eskalationsbereitschaft Russlands. "Und es ist mir vor diesem Hintergrund, ich sage es sehr offen, unbegreiflich, wie Sie von ganz links und ganz rechts trotzdem bis zum heutigen Tag das Spiel der Verharmlosung treiben."
EU-Gipfel berät über Schutz der Wirtschaft und Haushalt
Hauptthema von Merz' Regierungserklärung war der EU-Gipfel, zu dem er am Abend nach Brüssel reist. Dabei geht es unter anderem um den EU-Haushalt und neue Schutzmechanismen für die europäische Wirtschaft. "Wir sehen nicht länger tatenlos zu, wenn andere Staaten durch hohe Subventionen, künstlich abgewertete Währungen, Überkapazitäten und aggressive Preissetzung unserer Wirtschaft schaden", sagte Merz.
Die Aussage dürfte sich wohl vor allem auf China beziehen. China wird vorgeworfen, den Markt durch staatliche Subventionen zu verzerren, Überkapazitäten zu erzeugen und so Dumpingpreise zu ermöglichen, mit denen europäische Firmen nicht mithalten können.
Merz sagte weiter: "Wer mit uns den Handelskonflikt sucht, der wird erfahren, dass wir uns jetzt zur Wehr setzen, und zwar mit angemessenen Reaktionen."

title: Angriff auf Kyjiw - Selenskyj beklagt fehlende Vorwarnung
content_c:
Angriff auf Kyjiw - Selenskyj beklagt fehlende Vorwarnung
14. Oktober 2026
Unmittelbar nach Auslösung des Luftalarms wegen herannahender ballistischer Raketen waren schon die ersten Explosionen in Kyjiw zu hören. Ein neunstöckiges Wohngebäude im Bezirk Desnjanskyj ging nach einem Treffer in Flammen auf. Laut Bürgermeister Vitali Klitschko gab es mindestens zwei Tote und mehr als 20 Verletzte.
Wie schon am Vortag hätten die internationalen Partner auch diesmal keine Warnhinweise auf einfliegende Raketen gegeben, sagte der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj. Die Geschosse seien quasi erst im Anflug auf die ukrainische Hauptstadt von den Radaren entdeckt worden. Außer dem Wohnblock sei auch ein Heizkraftwerk getroffen worden.
US-Regierung bestreitet Vorwürfe
Selenskyj beklagte, den russischen Angreifern werde es zu einfach gemacht. "Das ist überhaupt nicht gerecht, wenn sie Energieanlagen zerstören und die Ukraine nicht einmal Warnungen vor dem Start von ballistischen Raketen erhält", schrieb er im Nachrichtendienst Telegram. Die US-Regierung bestritt Vorwürfe, wonach militärische Informationen nicht mehr mit den Ukrainern geteilt würden.
Die Ukraine verließ sich in ihrem seit 2022 andauernden Abwehrkampf gegen Russland bislang vor allem auf Aufklärungsdaten des US-Militärs, aber auch auf die anderer NATO-Mitgliedstaaten. Zuletzt traten jedoch wieder Spannungen zwischen den Regierungen in Kyjiw und Washington offen zutage.
Trump will Ende der gegenseitigen Angriffe
Russland attackiert die Energieversorgung in Kyjiw seit Wochen verstärkt. Die Angriffe führten bereits zu Strom- und Wasserausfällen und brachten zeitweise auch den U-Bahn-Verkehr zum Erliegen. Als Reaktion greift die Ukraine Energieinfrastruktur in Russland und nimmt dabei unter anderem Raffinerien und Öldepots ins Visier. US-Präsident Donald Trump, der wegen der infolge des Iran-Kriegs hohen Spritpreise unter Druck steht, verlangt ein Ende dieser Angriffe.
Trump hatte am Freitag eine Vereinbarung mit Kreml-Chef Wladimir Putin über die Lieferung von russischem Diesel bekanntgegeben. Mit dem umstrittenen Diesel-Deal setzte sich Trump über die vom Westen und den USA verhängten Russland-Sanktionen hinweg. Nach Kritik Selenskyjs an der Vereinbarung forderte Trump dessen Ablösung und Neuwahlen in der Ukraine.
Am Sonntag erklärte Trump dann, Russland und die Ukraine hätten einer Einstellung der Angriffe auf Energieanlagen im jeweils anderen Land zugestimmt. Moskau bestätigte eine solche Vereinbarung nicht.
gri/pgr (dpa, afp)
Redaktionsschluss: 15.45 Uhr (MESZ) - dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert.
